concepts.name: Nature of conflict
concepts.summary: Recognise conflict as a perceived incompatibility of needs, goals or values between people, and that it is normal and can be constructive or destructive.

concepts.name: Common sources of conflict
concepts.summary: Explain how scarce resources, unclear roles, differing values, poor communication and personality clashes commonly spark disputes.

concepts.name: Conflict escalation signs
concepts.summary: Spot early signs such as raised voices, withdrawal, sarcasm and blaming that show a disagreement is intensifying.

concepts.name: Five conflict styles
concepts.summary: Name the avoiding, accommodating, competing, compromising and collaborating styles and describe each in a sentence.

concepts.name: Listening before responding
concepts.summary: Understand why letting the other person finish and paying attention to them, without planning a rebuttal, lowers tension.

concepts.name: Calm-down pause
concepts.summary: Explain why stepping away briefly when emotions run high helps a discussion resume productively.

misconceptions.text: Conflict is always bad and a sign that a relationship or team is failing.
Listening just means staying quiet until it is your turn to talk.
Avoiding a disagreement makes it go away on its own.

concepts.name: Active listening techniques
concepts.summary: Apply paraphrasing, open questions, summarising and nonverbal attentiveness to show and check understanding in a real disagreement.

concepts.name: I-statements
concepts.summary: Construct statements describing behaviour, your feeling and its impact without accusing, instead of using you-statements.

concepts.name: Matching styles to situations
concepts.summary: Pick a conflict style suited to simple situations, such as accommodating on trivial issues or competing in an emergency.

concepts.name: De-escalation phrases
concepts.summary: Use calm tone, acknowledgement of feelings and lowered pace to reduce intensity when someone is angry.

concepts.name: Asking clarifying questions
concepts.summary: Ask neutral, open questions to uncover facts and needs rather than assuming the other's motives.

concepts.name: Positions versus interests
concepts.summary: Distinguish what someone says they want (position) from the underlying needs and concerns (interests) that drive it.

misconceptions.text: An I-statement is just a you-accusation with 'I feel' placed in front of it.
Paraphrasing what someone said means you agree with them.
The other person's stated demand is what they truly need.

concepts.name: Root cause analysis of disputes
concepts.summary: Separate triggers from deeper causes such as structural, relational, data or value issues by examining a conflict's history and context.

concepts.name: Interest mapping
concepts.summary: Analyse each party's interests to find common, compatible and conflicting ones as the basis for solutions.

concepts.name: Win-win option generation
concepts.summary: Generate multiple options that meet both parties' interests, using brainstorming before judging proposals.

concepts.name: Structured difficult conversation
concepts.summary: Prepare and run a conversation by setting purpose, describing facts, sharing impact, inviting the other view and agreeing next steps.

concepts.name: Workplace dispute dynamics
concepts.summary: Analyse how hierarchy, role ambiguity, policy and escalation channels such as HR shape disputes at work.

concepts.name: Family conflict patterns
concepts.summary: Identify recurring cycles such as pursue-withdraw, triangulation and old grievances in family disputes.

concepts.name: Objective criteria for fairness
concepts.summary: Use external standards such as market rates, precedent or policy to judge proposals instead of contests of will.

misconceptions.text: Compromise is the best outcome because both sides give something up equally.
The event that set off the argument is its root cause.
Every interest conflict is zero-sum, so one side must lose for the other to win.

concepts.name: Mediation process stages
concepts.summary: Analyse the phases of mediation, from opening and storytelling through issue framing, option generation and agreement, and what each accomplishes.

concepts.name: Mediator neutrality and impartiality
concepts.summary: Judge whether a mediator's conduct preserves impartiality, confidentiality and party self-determination.

concepts.name: Power imbalance management
concepts.summary: Assess how unequal power distorts negotiation and decide on safeguards or whether mediation is appropriate.

concepts.name: Choosing intervention level
aliases: when to bring in a third party
concepts.summary: Evaluate when to self-resolve, facilitate, mediate, arbitrate or escalate, given the stakes, power balance and relationship.

concepts.name: Reframing and caucusing
concepts.summary: Analyse how reframing accusations into shared problems and separate private meetings unlock stalled talks.

concepts.name: Evaluating settlement durability
concepts.summary: Assess whether an agreement is specific, realistic, mutually owned and equipped with follow-up so it will hold.

misconceptions.text: A mediator decides who is right and imposes the outcome.
A signed agreement means the conflict is resolved.
Mediation works equally well in every dispute regardless of power or safety concerns.

concepts.name: Designing dispute resolution systems
concepts.summary: Create a tiered system of negotiation, mediation and arbitration channels that fits an organisation's culture and prevents disputes from escalating.

concepts.name: Cultural variation in conflict
concepts.summary: Evaluate how culture shapes norms about directness, face, authority and emotion, and adapt approach accordingly.

concepts.name: Multi-party dispute facilitation
concepts.summary: Design processes for disputes with many stakeholders, managing coalitions, representation and sequencing of issues.

concepts.name: Critiquing resolution approaches
concepts.summary: Weigh interest-based, transformative, narrative and rights-based approaches against their assumptions and fit for a dispute.

concepts.name: Entrenched conflict transformation
concepts.summary: Devise strategies for long-running disputes involving identity, history and trust damage, going beyond settlement to relational change.

concepts.name: Own bias and role reflection
concepts.summary: Evaluate your own triggers, biases and habitual style to improve practice and coach others.

misconceptions.text: Interest-based negotiation works the same way in every culture.
Every long-running conflict can be resolved by finding the right win-win deal.
An experienced practitioner is free of bias in the disputes they handle.
